meta.translators: Alexandrian Jewish translators (2nd c. BCE) with later revisions

preamble.summary: LXX Song of Songs tracks MT closely. The book is not quoted in the NT. Its Greek reception-history, however, is extraordinary: Origen's three-book commentary and ten-book homilies on Song of Songs established the allegorical reading of the book as the love-song between Christ and the Church — a reading that would dominate Christian exegesis for over a thousand years. The LXX's specific vocabulary choices shaped this tradition at every point.
preamble.notable_variants: The superlative title 'song of songs' rendered aisma aismatōn in LXX; the 'love is as strong as death' of 8:6 in its LXX form that circulated as the book's epigraph in Hellenistic Jewish poetic piety; the botanical vocabulary of 2:1 rendered interpretively that gave later Western tradition 'the rose of Sharon.'
preamble.theological_legacy: The allegorical Christian reading of Song of Songs — Christ-and-church, soul-and-God — was constructed in Greek on the base of LXX vocabulary. Origen read the Song's phileō, agapaō, philēma, nymphē as the Greek words of a spiritual love-narrative. The LXX text made the allegory possible; the Hebrew original, for all its theological depth, does not carry the same Greek theological vocabulary.

renderings.lxx_reading: ᾆσμα ᾀσμάτων ὅ ἐστιν τῷ Σαλωμων
renderings.mt_rendering: The finest song, which is Solomon's
renderings.lxx_rendering: A song of songs, which is Solomon's
notes: The LXX preserves the Hebrew superlative construction shir ha-shirim ('the song of songs' = 'the finest song, the song par excellence') with the matching Greek aisma aismatōn.

TCR renders the superlative force as 'the finest song.' The LXX preserves the literal double-plural idiom, which the Vulgate inherits as canticum canticorum and the KJV as 'song of songs.' Either rendering captures the sense that this is the preeminent song.

renderings.lxx_reading: ἐγὼ ἄνθος τοῦ πεδίου κρίνον τῶν κοιλάδων
renderings.mt_rendering: I am a wildflower of the Sharon, a lily of the valleys
renderings.lxx_rendering: I am a flower of the plain, a lily of the valleys
notes: Hebrew chavatselet (probably a crocus, meadow saffron, or specific local flower) is rendered generically anthos tou pediou ('flower of the plain'). The English 'rose of Sharon' is a much later tradition (post-Vulgate, possibly via English herbal vocabulary) and represents neither the Hebrew nor the LXX accurately.
Hebrew shoshannat ha-amaqim — 'lily of the valleys' — is rendered word-for-word in LXX and carried into Latin and European vernaculars as one of the book's famous phrases.

renderings.mt_reading: עַזָּה כַמָּוֶת אַהֲבָה קָשָׁה כִשְׁאוֹל קִנְאָה רְשָׁפֶיהָ רִשְׁפֵּי אֵשׁ שַׁלְהֶבֶתְיָה
renderings.lxx_reading: κραταιὰ ὡς θάνατος ἀγάπη σκληρὸς ὡς ᾅδης ζῆλος περίπτερα αὐτῆς περίπτερα πυρὸς φλόγες αὐτῆς
renderings.mt_rendering: love is as fierce as death, passion as relentless as the grave. Its flames are flames of fire, the very blaze of Yah
renderings.lxx_rendering: love is strong as death, jealousy is hard as Hades; her flames are flames of fire, her fires
notes: The Hebrew ends the verse with shalhevetyah — a compound of shalhevet ('flame') and yah (the short form of YHWH) — 'the very flame of the LORD' or 'a flame of Yah.' This is one of only a few occurrences of the divine name in Song of Songs and the only one that most modern scholars accept as intended.
The LXX does not render yah as kyrios here but treats shalhevetyah as simply 'her flames' (phloges autēs). The divine-name reference is lost in the Greek.

The LXX's losing of yah may reflect a non-recognition of the compound, or a reluctance to use the divine name in what appeared to be a secular love poem. TCR preserves the divine-name recognition: 'the very blaze of Yah.'
This is one of the more poignant cases where the LXX's interpretive decision — whether accidental or deliberate — stripped a Hebrew text of its one moment of explicit divine reference.
